title: The bee (49–52)
hookLine: as the bee takes nectar and leaves the flower unharmed; look to your own faults, not others'
tomorrow: The lotus on the rubbish heap (53–59)

cards: Watch a bee in a garden for one minute. It lands on a flower, pushes in, takes what it came for, and lifts off. Then look at the flower.

Same petals, same color, same scent, still open for the next bee. If anything, it's better off: the bee carried its pollen along. A lot of taking doesn't work that way: something is used up, bruised, left worse.
The Dhammapada watched the same garden and found a whole way of living in it.

teach.h: TAKE, AND LEAVE THE FLOWER WHOLE.
teach.b: Verse forty-nine, in Müller's English: “As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.”

teach.h: THE MONK ON HIS ALMS ROUND.
teach.b: The first picture is a monk on his alms round.
He walks into the village, receives a little food from each house, and leaves without being a burden to anyone: taking only what's offered, leaving every household as whole as he found it.
But the verse reaches anyone who depends on others, which is everyone.
Can you take what you need, from your family, your coworkers, the earth, and leave them unharmed? Verse fifty turns the bee's attention inward.
Don't look at the faults of others, it says, what they've done and left undone. Look at what you yourself have done and left undone. The bee doesn't inspect the flower for flaws.
It takes the nectar and goes. Then verses fifty-one and fifty-two, a twin pair about words.
Verse fifty-one: “Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.”

Verse fifty-two is the flower with color and scent: good words from someone who lives them. You met that idea in the cowherd; the flower chapter gives it a new picture. So the bee teaches three things.
Take without harming. Mind your own faults, not the flower's. And let your words carry some scent: something lived behind them.

how: Theravada monks still go on alms rounds, receiving small amounts of food from many households, and teachers cite the bee verse as a picture of taking from the world without harm.

o: sharing all that you have with everyone else
taking what you need and leaving others unharmed
working hard all day without ever resting

games.q: match the pieces of verses forty-nine to fifty-two.
p: takes nectar, leaves the flower whole
the monk on his alms round

s: the bee verse pictures a sage moving through his village
like a monk on alms round, taking a little from each house and leaving no one burdened.
verse fifty says to point out other people's faults so they can improve
it says look at what you yourself have done and left undone.
verse fifty-one compares fine but fruitless words to a beautiful flower without scent
verse fifty-two is its twin: words with the scent of practice.

games.q: you're a monk on alms round. one house is poor and offers only a spoonful of rice. what fits the bee?
o: receive it gladly and move on, taking only what's offered.
games.why: the bee takes a little and leaves the flower whole. the alms round spreads the need so no house is burdened.

practice: Think of the places you'll take something from today: food from the kitchen, time and help from a coworker, patience from someone at home, water, power, a seat on the bus.

For each, imagine being the bee, taking what you need and leaving it whole: a thank-you, cleaning up after yourself, not taking the last of something. Choose one place, and hold that picture while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: The bee. Taking the nectar and leaving the flower unharmed: living among others without using them up.

orig.note: Pali: bee, from verse forty-nine: 'yathapi bhamaro puppham.'

carryVoice: Your line: the bee leaves the flower. Nectar taken, the flower left whole. See you tomorrow.
